name: Neo-fascism
summary: Neo-fascism is the family of radical right tendencies and groups that took up fascism after the Second World War. Its defining sources describe it as militantly nationalist, preferring authoritarian to democratic government and totally rejecting Marxist socialism and its egalitarian ethos, while also attacking liberal market capitalism and seeking a third way. From the 1950s it reached beyond the single nation towards a united Europe opposed to both the United States and the Soviet Union, with corporatist economic ideas and a spiritual, socially conservative view of life.
scope: Post-1945 neo-fascism as the reference works and scholarship define it: political tendencies and groups after the Second World War inspired by fascism (Treccani; Encyclopaedia Judaica), above all in Italy (the MSI and the groups around it such as Ordine Nuovo) and the transnational European neo-fascist right of the 1950s (Calvert; Castelli Gattinara et al.). Answers come only from what these defining sources state about neo-fascism and its tradition, never from a single party's or group's programme (MSI, CasaPound, Forza Nuova are other subjects) nor from interwar fascism; the Encyclopaedia Judaica keeps movements aiming at a Nazi-type racial dictatorship apart as neo-Nazism.

notes: Later pass (claude-opus-5-5, 2026-11-09) bringing the 2026-10-15 audit to rules 5, prompted by search traffic (closest ideology of Nick Fuentes). The first pass rested on Wikipedia (s1, s2), Eco's essay on fascism in general (s3, a broader ideology) and a CasaPound leader's interview (s4, one organisation's platform); every answer resting only on them was nulled or replaced from the defining sources, with the old version kept in reviewHistory. Neo-fascism has no canonical text and was never the official doctrine of a state, so it has no regime record; the defining sources are the reference entries and scholarship on neo-fascism as such, and party programmes (the MSI's 1946 ten points, quoted by Meriggi; CasaPound's and Forza Nuova's platforms) were read but not used as the ideology's own. Themes searched: government (democracy, elections, leadership, constitution), economy (corporatism, markets, welfare), world (Europe, the superpowers, NATO), society (religion, family, bioethics, immigration, race), means (violence, elections) and ecology. Blocked or closed: Britannica's neofascism section (403), Copsey's chapter 'Neo-Fascism: A Footnote to the Fascist Epoch?' (Springer bot check), the European Parliament's 1985 Evrigenis report on aei.pitt.edu (bot check), del Hierro and Domper's 'Fascism reimagined' PDF at Maastricht (403), Cassina Wolff's article on democracy and corporatism in Italian neo-fascist ideology (paywalled), and Cento Bull's Oxford Handbook chapter, Gregor's The Search for Neofascism and Camus and Lebourg (not open). The first pass's one missing statement (citizenship by descent, already added to the bank as diaspora-return-right) is dropped from this audit: its only evidence was the CasaPound interview, another subject's platform, which no longer opens (403) and does not discuss neo-fascism. Most statements stay null because the open scholarship defines neo-fascism by a handful of traits; the strands (MSI conservatives, Evolian traditionalists, the social left) differ on NATO, violence and elections.
